items: A Saudi national, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested for installing a hidden audio recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room, raising security concerns in AI research.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday, October 13.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.

OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.

The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan’s personal bag.
OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.
The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the company said.
OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

“Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release.
A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said.
Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile.

Separately, the Information reported that OpenAI was in early talks to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.
OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information.

The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could raise safety concerns. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: 'Big man, are you playing politics with your products again?' Poland's Sikorski taunts Musk
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has taken to X to confront the platform’s billionaire owner Elon Musk over reported restrictions to Starlink in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Poland helps Ukraine to foot the bill for Starlink, which provides crucial internet connectivity to Kyiv and its military, and says it pays some $50m a year.
Sikorski said:
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The pair repeatedly clashed in the past, with annoyed Musk telling Sikorski last year to be “quiet.”
Italy's Meloni criticises US-Russia diesel deal as 'very risky choice'
Meanwhile, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the US deal with Russia over diesel supply is “a very risky choice,” with “clear” risks.

blocks.caption: PM Giorgia Meloni speaks in the Italian parliament in Rome earlier today. Photograph: Mauro Scrobogna/LaPresse/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The outcome ​of this decision is ‌uncertain, while the ‌risks are clear,” Meloni told the Italian parliament.
“It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions,” she added.
The Italian PM also returned to the idea that the EU27 should appoint “an authoritative figure” to lead talks with Russia and Ukraine.
The overnight attacks killed at least three people in Kyiv, authorities said.
Mayor Vitaly Klitschko reported overnight that “a massive ballistic missile strike” against the capital hit its energy facilities, causing power outages across the city.
Wednesday’s Russian attacks also targeted state railway facilities in five regions across Ukraine, said prime ⁠minister Sergii Koretskyi.
Morning opening: Russia showing 'ostentatious disrespect' towards US with attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy says

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, after a night of relentless attacks on Ukraine’s infrastructure, despite Donald Trump’s claims of an energy ceasefire.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian firefighters extinguish a blaze at the site of a Russian missile strike at an apartment building in Kyiv. Photograph: Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale,” he said.
At least 600,000 people were left without power this morning, with temperatures falling below 10 degrees Celsius in Kyiv.

Meanwhile, a senior aide to Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has been left struggling after Starlink satellite connection speeds were apparently restricted, complicating military operations on the ground.
Serhii Beskrestnov, widely known by his call sign, Flash, said:

“Our defence forces received no warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy is expected in London today for talks with the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, so we will probably hear more from him.

Elsewhere, Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte will visit Estonia this morning, and Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to address the Bundestag with a statement on the EU and Ukraine this afternoon.
And Pope Leo had a “peaceful night” at Rome’s Gemelli hospital after yesterday’s surgery which confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
Lots to cover.
I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.
It’s Wednesday, 14 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football
articles.summary: Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and history at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for greater structure globally.

image.caption: North Korea have one of the best youth teams in women's football in the world, but questions are being asked about baseline support for women in the gameImage: IPA Sport/ABACA/IMAGO

blocks.text: At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first on the continent, will be the last with 32 teams but is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is a moment of history as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.
Women's game falling short on global standards

But even the handful of players who makes it from these youth tournaments to a professional career, making a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.
The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The average club contract length is 1.6 years.

"If you know the global average is $2,600, but then the median drops by $1,000 to just over $1,600 so that that gives you an indication of the kind of the salary range that that we're dealing with here," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"I think what you also find in the in the women's game is the the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," said Brown. "In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and and not being paid paid at all."
With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement. "Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures – including extra workload and social media abuse - but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich are one of the biggest clubs in the world, but Germany also has gaps when it comes to baseline support for women playing professional footballImage: O. Behrendt/Contrast/IMAGO

blocks.text: Germany aiming to be example of development

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier - in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year - the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German FA (DFB) rule reveals that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.
Ultimately, the faster the game grows the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

articles.title: Child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as ‘safe’ day after she was admitted to hospital in coma
articles.summary:
Inquest into the death of eight-year-old Queensland girl who was denied insulin by her religious parents is told her case was complex

A child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth…

blocks.text: A child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as “safe” one day after she arrived at hospital in a coma and nearly died due to the neglect of her parents, a coroner’s court has heard.

A Queensland coronial inquest heard evidence on Tuesday from one of the two child safety officers who ultimately decided to return the then six-year-old type 1 diabetic to the care of her parents at their home in Toowoomba.
She died there on 7 Jan 2022 while her mother, Kerrie, father Jason and other members of their small religious sect prayed for her miraculous healing or resurrection.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

The child safety officer was given the duty of investigating Elizabeth’s home after she presented to Toowoomba hospital in a coma suffering from diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July 2019. He later became her case worker.

Just one day later – after she was transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane – another child safety officer who assisted him completed an initial safety assessment of Elizabeth. She marked her “safe”.
But her colleague told the court on Wednesday that Elizabeth should have been recorded as “unsafe” because they didn’t have enough information about her circumstances at the time.
Elizabeth was later assessed as a child in need of protection, a legal standard under the child safety act.
In 2021, both Jason and Kerrie were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to their daughter as a result of the 2019 incident, and Kerrie jailed.

The child safety officer later had a conversation with a doctor from the Queensland children’s hospital who told him Elizabeth was lucky not to have died and that Kerrie had not shown remorse as a result of the incident.
The doctor said Kerrie continued to not believe in medicine and that it would be unsafe for her daughter to live with her until she changed her views, the inquest heard.
“The pressure on dad around such strong religious beliefs will be difficult,” the doctor told him, according to his contemporaneous notes presented in court on Wednesday.
“The team feel that the only way to force mum to see the concerns may be for Elizabeth to be out of home.”
Elizabeth was sent home despite the objections of the Brisbane-based specialist pediatric doctors.
The doctor told the court on Monday that she felt “stonewalled” by the officer after raising concerns about Elizabeth’s safety at home.

Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary arrangement that allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard.
after newsletter promotion
On Wednesday, the child safety officer said that the safety plan they adopted for Elizabeth “in hindsight, could have been more robust”.
But he said he didn’t have a clear recollection of a meeting in which they discussed the idea of adopting the plan.

“I do recall being in two minds about the best outcome for Elizabeth and her siblings specifically Elizabeth being able to remain at home and connected with her family or out of home,” he said in a written statement provided to the court.
He said it was a difficult decision and that there were practical considerations of how to manage the complex case.
The child safety officer said it was significant that Jason had repeatedly committed to provide insulin for his daughter. Elizabeth required daily insulin injections to live.

The inquest previously heard Jason, a long-time skeptic of his wife’s religion, subsequently provided medical attention for Elizabeth for two years. But he ceased doing so after being convinced to convert and then to stop treating her by the members of the group and stopped her insulin in late 2021, causing her death.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: China must stop 'predatory activities' for DND to restore military dialogue -- Teodoro
articles.summary: China must first stop its “predatory activities” in the West Philippine Sea before the Department of National Defense (DND) will restore the military-to-military dialogue between Manila and Beijing,…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 4:00pm

China must first stop its “predatory activities” in the West Philippine Sea before the Department of National Defense (DND) will restore the military-to-military dialogue between Manila and Beijing, Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro Jr. said Wednesday.

“All their actions now from their messaging to their assertion of disputed sovereignty and jurisdiction over areas where they have no rights to do so, they must turn back from that because there is no basis whatsoever in international law and in UNCLOS,” he said.

“They must stop their predatory activities in the Pacific and in the West Philippine Sea which is a threat to regional and global security. It is obviously a threat to regional security and several countries have voiced concern about this,” he stressed.
He issued the remark when asked about specific actions that China must take in order to prompt him to restore communications.
This came after the Chinese Embassy in Manila accused Teodoro of suspending the military-to-military communication between China and Philippines for his “political self interests.”
Teodoro, however, said that the dialogue between Manila and Beijing was severed three years ago.
“That is inaccurate because that happened about three years ago. So hindi ngayon nangyari iyon. Matagal na ‘yun kasi nga inaabuso nila ‘yung mga proseso natin,” he said.
(That is inaccurate because that happened about three years ago. So that did not happen now. That was a long time ago because they are abusing our processes.)
“So hininto ko ‘yung direct communication except for one line,” he added.
(So I stopped direct communication except for one line.)
For his part, Teodoro said he did not see the value in a dialogue with Beijing.
“Kasi nga, walang structure ‘yung communications flow at ito ay naaubos lamang. So hindi bagong desisyon ito. Matagal na ito kaya hindi ko alam kung [bakit] parang kahapon lang nangyari,” he said.

(Since there was no structure in the communications flow and it was simply being depleted. So this is not a new decision. This happened a long time ago, which is why I don’t know why it seems like it only happened yesterday.)
Meanwhile, Teodoro expressed disappointment with comments that there will be a war with China due to the suspension.
He said the DND is merely standing up for the country’s sovereignty.

“Hindi giyera ang pinag uusapan natin eh. Naninindigan lang tayo sa pride ng bansa natin. Ngayon kung walang pride ang isang tao na naninindigan ang AFP at saka DND para sa soberanya niya sa abot ng ating makakaya, anong klase tayong mamamayan?” he said.

(We’re not talking about war. We’re just standing firm on our country’s pride. Now, if a person has no pride in standing firm as the AFP and the DND do for our sovereignty to the best of our ability, what kind of citizens are we?)
Teodoro also said that such remarks are insulting to Filipino troops.
“‘Yung mga nang ga-gaslighting— kailangan alamin na rin ng mga taong bayan natin ‘yung mga gaslighting na ‘yan is our worst enemy. At minsan ang Filipino is our worst enemy sometimes,” he said.
(Those who are gaslighting—we also need our people to understand that gaslighting is our worst enemy. And sometimes, the Filipino is our worst enemy sometimes.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Burnham says UK to increase supply of anti-drone missiles to Ukraine, ahead of PMQs and Zelenskyy – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Prime minister to face MPs at PMQs before hosting Ukraine’s president in London

Good morning. Andy Burnham is taking PMQs this afternoon, but he will regard his most…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham is taking PMQs this afternoon, but he will regard his most important engagement as the meeting he has with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, later in No 10. Peter Walker has a preview.

When Keir Starmer talked about his best achievements as PM, he said one of the things he was most proud of was being able to embrace Zelenskyy outside No 10 only 24 hours after President Trump humiliated him in the Oval Office, in what was a moving and unequivocal show of British support for Ukraine at a moment of peril. The circumstances are not exactly the same today, but Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced at the weekend, and – again – Burnham is signalling that, if Ukraine cannot always rely on Washington, it can rely on London.
In an overnight statement, Burnham said:

double quotation markOur rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.

Burnham is also announcing that the UK will “accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond.” No 10 says:

double quotation markThe [Russian] drones are faster and can fly far higher than propeller-driven Shaheds, making them harder to detect and destroy before they hit targets. The UK has already committed £1.6 billion to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine over the next four years and will accelerate £10m of the £45m package of missiles announced today to meet Ukraine’s most urgent winter requirements.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10.30am: Dominic Cummings, Boris Johnson’s former chief adviser, gives evidence to the Lords constitution committee on constitutional safeguards.
Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.

After 12.30pm: MPs debate a Tory opposition day motion saying that the government should not place asylum seekers in a military camp near Piddington, and that it should “withdraw from the European convention on human rights in order to deport illegal migrants”.
Afternoon: Burnham hosts Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, in Downing Street.
3pm: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, gives evidence to the Commons energy committee.

articles.title: Italian wine thieves nab $8M of vino in heist. Here's why wine is a 'great target'
articles.summary: A winery in Tuscany is reeling after thieves made off with about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy's most prized wines last week in what the producer described as the country’s largest wine theft on…

image.caption: This photo released Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, by the Marchesi Antinori winery shows, from left, bottles of 2023 Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso red wine, among some 30,000 bottles stolen that are worth an estimated 5 million euros, or $7.96 million Cdn. (Marchesi Antinori/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: First, they came for the cheese. Then, they came for the olive oil and the butter.
Now, thieves have come for the good wine, and we have to say these recent heists are starting to feel personal if you're the type of person who enjoys a little treat.

Last week, a winery in Tuscany revealed that thieves made off with about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy's most prized wines in what the producer described as the country’s largest wine theft on record. The sought-after 2023 vintages — including Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso — are worth an estimated five million euros, or just under $8 million Cdn.
"A theft of this size and value has never occurred in Italy," Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive of Italy's largest family-run winemaker, Marchesi Antinori, told the Associated Press on Friday.

While the theft may be Italy's largest, and perhaps most brazen, it's also just the most recent. Last month, 3,000 bottles of Barolo were stolen in the northern Piedmont region, according to French news site Le Monde. In late June, thieves hit the renowned Banfi winery in Montalcino, nabbing 3,000 bottles of sparkling wine, noted an Italian news site.
It's also not just an Italian problem.

Globally, some notable recent heists include the thief who made off with about 800 bottles from a California wine shop in 2023, a couple who stole about $1.7 million US worth of rare wine from a Michelin-starred restaurant in Spain in 2021, and criminals who stole 500 kilograms' worth of white wine grapes — equivalent to about 350 bottles of wine — from a Quebec vineyard in 2020.

Benoit Giroussens, the vineyard manager at Vignoble et Cidrerie Coteau Rougemont in Quebec, is pictured in 2020 after thieves ripped the grapes off the vines and stuffed them into garbage bags. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

Heists and large-scale thefts are on the rise, said Rod Phillips, a history professor at Carleton University in Ottawa who specializes in the history of alcohol. Fine wine has a big black market, Phillips said, and plenty of people are willing to purchase expensive wine at a lower price.
"There are various channels to selling fine wine and I think they're all very receptive these days, now that everybody is under financial pressure," Phillips told CBC News.

It also packs a lot of value into a small amount of product, with a single case sometime worth thousands of euros, said wine expert Natalie MacLean. It doesn't spoil, either, meaning thieves can sit on it for years before selling — and unlike a painting, a case of wine isn't one of a kind.
"I do think it's a trend," MacLean told CBC News. "People are looking to cash in and wine is a great target."
What happened in Italy?
The most recent theft targeted Marchesi Antinori’s facility near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, and appeared to be planned down to the finest detail, according to Italian news site Rai news.

Seven thieves disabled the alarm system and surveillance cameras, then used the company's own forklifts to load two trucks with wine and then flee into the night, Cotarella, the winery chief executive, told the Associated Press.

items: The grape escape: Thieves steal 500 kilos from Rougemont winery
Why so many cheese heists? As B.C. cops foil another, here's why cheese is so valuable

blocks.text: Depending on how they package them, that's about 2,500 cases of wine to lift and load, Phillips noted.
"You don't move that very quickly ... and it's obviously got to be very well planned," he said.

Police and Carabinieri officers are examining surveillance footage and other evidence, the Associated Press said. CBC News has reached out to the winery, and the local police department and Carabinieri for more information and not yet heard back.
A view shows vineyards and the exterior of the Marchesi Antinori winery in Bargino, near Florence, Italy, in this undated handout image. (Marchesi Antinori Press/Handout/Reuters)

The stolen bottles were all from the 2023 vintage and are typically sold at a retail price of between 150 and 500 euros each (between $240 and $800 Cdn). They included about 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Antinori’s flagship wines.
Antinori makes only 60,000 to 70,000 bottles of Solaia a year, explained MacLean, the wine expert. That's about a sixth of a vintage gone in one night.
"The Solaia loss is staggering," she said.
The theft was discovered Oct. 5, but the company made it public on Oct. 9 to avoid interfering with the investigation.
"People at the winery were crying,” Cotarella told the Financial Review.
"It’s not just the value of the wine — it’s something more. We can survive without this wine, but what makes me so sad is the fact that this could happen to us."
A short history of recent heists

Up until recently, most wine crime usually involved fraud as opposed to theft, said Phillips, the historian. Counterfeit Canadian ice wines made and sold in China, for instance, damaged sales in Ontario some 20 years ago.
"These heists are more of a recent phenomenon," he said.

items: Over $1M worth of olive oil stolen from transport company in Montreal
Thieves stole 100,000 organic eggs off a trailer in Pennsylvania. Police are scrambling

blocks.text: It's also not just wine that thieves are getting their hands on. In August, thieves made off with 40,000 pounds of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer in Southern California. Police estimated that the stolen beer was worth almost $100,000 Cdn.
There have also been a number of major food-related heists recently, which some analysts have linked to rising food prices.

Last year, Montreal police said over $1 million worth of olive oil was stolen after a delivery involving two transport companies in the city never arrived at its destination in Ontario. Police in Ontario that year also charged six people with a string of butter and ghee thefts, with losses of more than $60,000.
#TheMoment B.C. police foiled a nearly $13K cheese heist

Also in 2025, 40,000 oysters, lobster worth $568,000 Cdn and a cache of crab meat all were stolen in separate incidents within weeks of each other in New England. Meanwhile, in Pennsylvania, someone stole 100,000 organic eggs valued at about $57,000 Cdn off the back of a distribution trailer.
Of course, the cheese world is still reeling after a 2024 U.K. cheese heist that saw con artists make off with more than £300,000 (or more than $540,000 Cdn) in cloth-bound, award-winning cheddar.

The same year, B.C. RCMP revealed they'd recently foiled an attempted cheese heist at a Whole Foods in North Vancouver. They'd been on patrol Sept. 29, 2024, when they found a cart full of cheese outside the grocery store. A suspect fled on foot, leaving $12,800 worth of cheese behind.
But Canada's most famous food theft is likely the notorious 2012 maple syrup heist, where thieves in Quebec stole more than $18 million worth of the sweet stuff.

articles.title: A fridge hack spoiled food in hundreds of French supermarkets. Cybersecurity experts say it's a wake-up call
articles.summary: The cyberattack on French supermarkets earlier this week that left hundreds of fridges worth of food spoiled should be a wake-up call about the vulnerabilities of digitized systems and devices that…

image.caption: Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarché supermarket in Paris on Tuesday, the day after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains. (Lucien Libert/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

The cyberattack on French supermarkets earlier this week that left hundreds of fridges worth of food spoiled should be a wake-up call about the vulnerabilities of digitized systems and devices that are connected to the internet, cybersecurity experts say.
Hackers may have targeted out-of-date firmware that remotely controls fridge temperatures

The cyberattack on French supermarkets earlier this week that ultimately spoiled hundreds of fridges worth of food should be a wake-up call about the vulnerabilities of digitized systems and devices that are connected to the internet, cybersecurity experts say.
"The more we rely on connected technology, the more we need to keep in mind the crucial aspect that is their security and privacy," said Montreal-based cybersecurity expert Steven Lachance.

The attack appeared to target centralized control systems that allow the temperature of fridges to be changed remotely. Hackers were able to access those controls and jack up fridge temperatures at hundreds of grocery stores — in some cases as high as 50 C — causing their contents to spoil, and potentially causing fires.

The Paris prosecutor's office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack to determine the extent of the damage and pin down the hackers behind it. No group has claimed responsibility so far, nor was there a ransom demand, according to Reuters.

items: Cyberattack defrosts French supermarket freezers, spoiling food at 100s of stores

blocks.text: Here's what you need to know about the supermarket cyberattack and what it shows about the vulnerability of our tech — from commercial systems to household devices.
What happened in France?

Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak says the fridges in stores are usually connected to the internet through a centralized panel that allows metrics like temperature to be monitored and adjusted remotely.

Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Coopérative U, one of the affected French grocery store chains, said on social media that its fridges are connected to the internet in this way in order to monitor temperatures around the clock "in the event of an anomaly."
On Monday, France's national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said it was aware of numerous refrigerator control panels being compromised.
ANSSI said the remote monitoring systems targeted were made by a Dutch company called Danfoss. The cybersecurity agency later said similar systems made by Copeland and Dixell were also targeted.

View of empty refrigerators at the frozen food aisle inside an Intermarché supermarket in Paris on Tuesday. The placard reads: "Important information. Our store has been hacked, and our refrigeration system has been affected." (Lucien Libert/Reuters)
Danfoss told news agencies on Monday that the affected units were running "outdated firmware," or had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates."

Cybersecurity firm ​Claroty published a report in August detailing a vulnerability with Danfoss's firmware that could allow hackers to bypass the standard login process and gain access in order to make changes remotely. Danfoss released a patch to fix the vulnerability shortly afterwards and urged users to install it.
"These vulnerabilities should be considered serious," the company said in its security advisory at the time.

The exact mechanism used to hack the fridge controllers in France is still unknown, but experts say it appears as though a failure to implement Danfoss's updates, as well as interfaces being left open to the internet, enabled it.
Kotak says out-of-date firmware in particular would have made the hack easy to pull off.
Firmware updates are sent out once a vulnerability has been detected — so when customers are made aware they need to implement an update, hackers become aware of the problem, too.
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter
"As a hacker, you will be able to know exactly what those vulnerabilities are and write code to exploit those exact vulnerabilities," Kotak said.
For that reason, Kotak says, implementing security updates quickly is really important.
Are such attacks on the food system common?
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told the country's parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected.
He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged the attack "touches the heart of our food security."

items: Hacker took 100,000 documents in 2025 'cyber incident,' Kingston Police say
Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case

blocks.text: But Kotak points out this is not the first such attack on the food distribution system. In 2021, for example, JBS — a major global supplier of meats — was hit by a cyberattack that temporarily shut down operations in Canada, the U.S. and Australia.
In 2025, United Natural Foods, Inc. — one of the biggest distributors of organic food — experienced an attack that led to significant shortages at Whole Foods.

Also Tuesday, Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said it was working to restore systems it had shut down following a security incident that began on Sunday night — one the Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it did not believe was linked to the French supermarket hack.
"This is something that unfortunately we're going to see more of," Kotak said. "What's happened in France needs to be a wake-up call that we need to take this seriously."
Cyberattack hits universities around the world including Canada

The food system's importance makes it a big potential target for an attack, he adds — and with processing, packaging and logistics becoming increasingly digitized, more possible avenues open up for hackers to try to gain access.
Kotak says helping food businesses become more digitally literate — so they employ safety-related updates and respond quickly when cyber incidents arise — is part of the solution.
"Cybersecurity … cannot be something that's a checkbox exercise. It needs to be something that's continuously being invested [in]" Kotak said.
What kind of devices are vulnerable?
Lachance, the Montreal-based expert, says the situation in France should serve as a reminder that any devices connected to the internet could in theory be hacked.

As internet connectivity becomes baked into more kinds of devices — both at a commercial level and a residential level with "smart" appliances, including thermostats, fridges, dishwashers and even lightbulbs — they can become vulnerable, he says.
"There is the convenience of this centralized control," Lachance said. But, "the security vulnerabilities that come with them [are] a growing problem and I suspect it's just going to become worse."
International team of researchers looked at how IoT devices interact with home networks

Lachance says devices that can record audio and video pose the most obvious privacy risks. Hacks have already happened, including a situation where hackers took control of some Ring cameras and used the tech to harass homeowners.
But hackers might also try to infiltrate smart devices in order to harvest passwords, or to gain access to other devices on the same network, Lachance says.

He says a solution is simply steering clear of smart devices, or keeping them disconnected from the internet in cases where that connectivity isn't necessary — especially in cheaper or lower-end devices, where he says security updates might not be prioritized by manufacturers.
For any devices that can record video or audio, Lachance recommends storing that data locally rather than making it accessible remotely.
"That's just the door waiting to be … broken in," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Labor’s bill to cut private health insurance rebate blocked by Greens over pensioner carve-out
articles.summary:
Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to end private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of Albanese government’s proposal

  • Get our

blocks.text: Labor’s bid to cut the private health insurance rebate for over-65s has been blocked in parliament, with the Greens insisting they will withhold support unless pensioners receive a carve-out from the new rules.
The proposed changes, which would take effect from April 2027, would save the federal budget $3bn.

It marks another defeat for a key cost-saving measure after the government was forced to back down on its plan to cap allied health payments for veterans which would have saved $748m over three years.
People who are 65 or over currently receive a larger rebate on their premium, with the rebate higher for those 70 and over.

The Greens, Coalition and crossbench senators teamed up in the Senate on Wednesday to block Labor’s bill. In a rare move, the bill was discharged from the upper house, meaning it will need to be reintroduced if Labor tries to push ahead.
The health minister, Mark Butler, said the government planned to reintroduce the same bill to parliament on Thursday.

“It is important that the parliament have a proper debate, that these really important questions for older Australians are not held hostage to political stunts, but instead that the elected members of the House of Representatives and elected senators take these issues seriously and debate them properly,” he said.

Almost 80,000 older Australians are expected to ditch their private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of the Albanese government’s proposal, according to health department modelling released under freedom of information laws.
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said the party would only offer its support for the changes if the government excluded pensioners.
“We say to Labor, if you want to bring this bill back … [by] carving out 1.2 million pensioners from this attack … come and talk to us,” he said.
“We will pass it in a heartbeat. But we will not be joining with Labor to punch down on pensioners in the middle of a cost of living crisis.”
Butler said the new Greens leadership “spied a political opportunity” to team up with the Coalition.
The chief executive of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, rejected the planned savings being linked to aged care funding commitments.

“Older Australians shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their health and paying for everyday essentials. Nor should they be asked to choose between affordable healthcare and a properly funded aged care system,” she said.
The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston, said the policy would have affected up to 1.5 million pensioners.
after newsletter promotion

“The idea that a government would have to cut the health system to need to pay for the aged care system … just reflects the fact of how much this government has lost control of their budget bottom line,” she said.
The proposal has been criticised by the states and territories, which warn their health services will come under increasing pressure.
The Victorian health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said she had raised concerns with Butler, vowing to oppose “any move that makes it harder for Victorians to get the care they need”.
“Any commonwealth savings shouldn’t come at the expense of older Victorians or simply shift pressure on to our public hospitals,” she said.

The New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, said the state was already experiencing “significant pressure” on its public health system due to the commonwealth’s failure to provide sufficient aged care placements.
“This is not good for [the aged] and they deserve better,” he said.
The Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, said the “additional pressure will come at the expense of the thousands of older Australians already stuck in hospitals right across the country”.

The Tasmanian health minister, Bridget Archer, said the federal government was “already refusing to provide solutions to get aged care patients out of hospital and this dog of a policy will make things even worse”.

articles.title: After prosecution’s bombshells, what does Sara’s defense have?
articles.summary: A lawyer tells Rappler what the defense 'bombshells' might be, when the impeachment trial resumes on November 9

blocks.text: There have been statements by Senate President Win Gatchalian that Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial may be done before the year ends. But with the prosecution’s decision to drop three of four impeachment articles against her, we might see the trial ending sooner than expected.

Lead public prosecutor Gerville Luistro said on Tuesday, October 13, that their evidence on unexplained wealth — the second article against Duterte — is enough to remove her from office and bar her from running in 2028.

Withdrawing an article during an impeachment trial is not really new as this happened in former chief justice Renato Corona’s trial. The House dropped five of eight articles. Eventually, Corona was ousted from his position — the first chief magistrate in the Philippines to have been convicted in an impeachment trial.
But there’s a difference between the two trials. The prosecution, in Corona’s case, withdrew the five articles before they could present their evidence for these articles.

In Duterte’s case, the prosecution had four. It presented evidence on alleged grave threats, misuse of confidential funds, and unexplained wealth. It never tackled the bribery allegation. And then Luistro announced that they would drop everything except the case on unexplained wealth.
“This has never happened before,” said defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa.
So, what will the defense’s next actions be after this rather surprising move from the prosecution?

To clarify, the defense did not object to the prosecution’s motion to withdraw the three articles. Poa and lead defense counsel Sheila Sison made it clear that this was the House’s prerogative — each party should have the final say on how it intends to present its own evidence.

In his ruling, impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero accepted the withdrawal with prejudice on the grave threats and confidential funds cases (meaning they can no longer be refiled by the prosecution), without prejudice to the bribery charge (since no evidence was ever presented in court).
One of the concerns of the defense, however, is whether they will be allowed to still present evidence on the two withdrawn articles.

“We had no problem with bribery because they never presented that. Our problem was the grave threats and confidential funds case because they already presented the testimonies of their witnesses there,” Poa said in Filipino.

“And we are not given now the opportunity to present rebuttal evidence through the testimonies of our witnesses…. Can we still present our evidence on those allegations or not? That’s one of the questions,” he added.
The defense will begin presenting its own evidence in November, but as Poa pointed out, it’s still unclear whether they will be able to present evidence on grave threats and confidential funds.
“There is no mechanism within the rules to allow the presentation of evidence on an article or on a charge that will not be voted upon by the court,” said Escudero.

Another sign that Duterte’s camp might not be given the opportunity is the relaxation of the sub judice rule. This principle bars parties — including the respondent — from publicly discussing the merits of the case to preserve the integrity of the proceedings. This gives Duterte’s camp the chance to present their evidence directly to the public, similar to what former senator Antonio Trillanes did after he was dropped as a prosecution witness. No holds barred.

blocks.caption: After prosecution’s bombshells, what does Sara’s defense have?

blocks.text: But the defense finds this problematic too.

“Now, I know that the court will say that, well, the respondent’s given the equal opportunity to do as she pleases with respect to the allegation. She can say a lot of things. Use all the platforms, in the words of the lead prosecutor, to avail of these platforms to present their evidence through these platforms,” said Sison.

But it would be unfair for the Vice President to be unable to present evidence in the impeachment court itself, the proper forum, according to Sison, because “the Vice President was held to this formal proceeding and in this court and honorable members of this court took their oaths, senators, judges.”
The parties — both the prosecution and the defense — cannot file a motion for reconsideration on the rulings made by the presiding officer. Only a senator-judge can.

Senator-judge Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said he is open to reconsidering the ruling on the abandonment of the sub judice rule. So, for now, Poa said they will first consult the Vice President and inform her about the court’s decision then inform the court about her position on the ruling.

Is the defense considering filing a petition for certiorari with the Supreme Court? This is a legal remedy used to seek review of grave abuse of discretion on the part of the impeachment court. If granted, this can overturn a ruling.
“As for certiorari, we are not considering a certiorari at this point. We are not talking about that,” said Poa.
In her manifestation before the court, Sison said the prosecution’s allegations must be tested.

“That prerogative to withdraw an accusation is not the power to suppress its rebuttal on the part of the respondent. The authority to streamline or to achieve speed in a trial is not the authority to diminish due process or to altogether disregard fundamental rules of fairness and the desire to reach a verdict,” said the lead defense counsel.
If there is no appeal and certiorari on the table, what could the bombshells of Duterte’s defense team be?

blocks.caption: After prosecution’s bombshells, what does Sara’s defense have?

blocks.text: “As implied by Attorney Sison a while ago, it might move for the dismissal of all articles of impeachment, citing mistrial. Or, as we discussed…. it might move for, or file a motion or demurrer to evidence on article 2, saying that as since the evidence relied upon by the prosecution is anchored solely on the false assumptions of Attorney Alex Cabrera, and the defense might mark it as false assumption, then they will also be moving for that,” lawyer and law professor Maria Lulu Reyes told Rappler.
Cabrera is the financial forensic analyst and prosecution witness who testified that Duterte’s unexplained wealth may reach P1.5 billion.

A demurrer to evidence, mentioned by Reyes, meanwhile, is filed when the defense believes that the prosecution’s evidence is weak enough that they don’t have to present their own. If granted, it will lead to an acquittal.
“So, either way, it’s to dismiss all the articles, not just the three that were mentioned today, but including article 2, the only remaining one,” Reyes added.

If her crystal ball is correct, the Jose Mari Chan Christmas meme, “Ilang tulog na lang…(Just a few more days left)” may be relevant to the impeachment trial. Ready na ba kayo? (Are you all ready?) – Rappler.com

articles.title: China alone is the troublemaker in the region - Teodoro
articles.summary: China alone is the troublemaker in the region – Teodoro MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Wednesday rejected Vice President Sara Duterte’s remark that the…

blocks.text: China alone is the troublemaker in the region – Teodoro

MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Wednesday rejected Vice President Sara Duterte’s remark that the Philippines was becoming a “troublemaker of Southeast Asia,” saying China was the one causing trouble in the region.
“Kaya ang troublemaker dito ay ang China lang,” Teodoro said in a Zoom interview with reporters. (China alone is the troublemaker here.)
Duterte made the remark on Monday, Oct. 12, while questioning the portrayal of China-linked business dealings as a national security threat.
Speaking to reporters during the Office of the Vice President’s anniversary celebration in Mandaluyong City, Duterte also cited a drug shipment bound for the Philippines from Laos and Thailand.
Asked about her statement, Teodoro pointed to the Philippines’ defense of its maritime rights, questioning how Filipino soldiers sacrificing to protect those rights could be called troublemakers.
He said the country’s rights at sea were tied to its future and sustainability.
“Obviously, nobody can say na ang Pilipinas ay ang nanggugulo dahil unang-una tayo ay mas maliit na bansa, ipinaglalaban lang natin ang kinabukasan ng ating bansa,” he said.
(Obviously, nobody can say the Philippines is causing trouble because, first of all, we are a smaller country. We are only fighting for our country’s future.)
Teodoro also cited other countries’ objections to Beijing’s conduct, saying China repeatedly dismissed criticism of its actions as provocative.
Asked whether Chinese rhetoric and influence operations could worsen ahead of the 2028 elections, he said the situation was already deteriorating.
“Wala pang eleksyon eh. Lumalala na eh,” he said. (There are no elections yet, and it is already getting worse.)

Teodoro warned that even slowing efforts to strengthen Philippine defenses could hurt the country’s ability to resist Chinese aggression and expansion. A policy reversal, he added, would be “damaging and disastrous” to its future.
On the business dealings raised in the same question, Teodoro said Filipinos are not prohibited from doing business with China.
But whether a public official was allowed to engage in particular transactions was a separate matter for the proper investigative authorities to determine, he said.
He added that dealings with China should be closely examined for legitimacy and propriety when they involved officials with a voice in matters affecting the country’s territorial integrity. /gsg

articles.title: Teodoro: China must drop baseless claims before military talks resume
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — China must abandon baseless maritime claims and demonstrate sincerity before direct military communications with the Philippines could resume, Defense Secretary Gilberto…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — China must abandon baseless maritime claims and demonstrate sincerity before direct military communications with the Philippines could resume, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said on Wednesday.
“Firstly, they must prove sincerity,” Teodoro said in a Zoom interview with reporters.

He said Beijing must retreat from assertions of sovereignty and jurisdiction over areas where it had no rights under international law and United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and stop what he called “predatory activities” threatening regional security.

His remarks addressed statements from the Chinese Embassy in Manila accusing him of closing military communication channels for “political self interests” and pushing frontline personnel closer to confrontation.
In a Facebook post on Tuesday, the embassy described cutting off military channels while refusing to face the potential consequences of conflict as “reckless and irresponsible.”
Teodoro disputed the portrayal of the suspension as a recent decision.
“That is inaccurate because that happened about three years ago,” he said.

He said he stopped direct communications after finding that the exchanges lacked structure and were being abused. He said the rest of communication were coursed through the Department of Foreign Affairs.

Teodoro clarified that the suspension covered direct communications between the Department of National Defense and its attached agencies and China’s defense establishment. Other avenues, including diplomatic channels, remained open.
He also rejected Beijing’s argument that military exchanges were needed to ease tensions.
“Sasabihin nila for de-escalation. Sino nag-e-escalate? Sila eh,” he said. (They will say it is for de-escalation. Who is escalating? They are.)

Asked about the embassy’s claim that his decision brought frontline forces closer to confrontation, Teodoro questioned whether the Philippines had any intention of going to war and accused China of using a false narrative.
The defense chief distinguished the suspension from Philippine Coast Guard communications with China, which he said should remain open for maritime safety and civilian law enforcement.

“The communications flow must remain open sa Coast Guard kasi civilian law enforcement ’yan,” he said. (Communications must remain open for the Coast Guard because that involves civilian law enforcement.)

Teodoro maintained that China’s maritime claims ran against the sovereign interests the Armed Forces of the Philippines was sworn to protect, saying he remained convinced that suspending direct military exchanges was the right decision. /mr

articles.title: John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
articles.summary:
Firms such as Amazon and eBay would be responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms

A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could…

blocks.text: A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget.
The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.

The move would target foreign retailers that have taken advantage of a lack of robust rules and enforcement to avoid paying VAT on their sales, according to the Times. It said Healey was expected to announce that these changes would be used to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops.
Online marketplaces would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for all retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, it was reported.
The development comes as pressure continues to grow on Andy Burnham and Healey to provide relief to struggling small businesses on the high street before the budget on 28 October.
Before he was elected in Makerfield, Burnham said he would increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high street retailers would not pay the tax.

While the government faces calls from many factions to cut tax, this week the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned Healey that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
The IFS said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.
In a boost for the Treasury, this week the International Monetary Fund upgraded its GDP growth forecast for the UK this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from its previous update in July.
after newsletter promotion

However the IMF also cautioned that Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte defends Sison against 'bully' tag in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday defended her lead defense counsel, Sheila Sison, against accusations of bullying from a private prosecutor in her impeachment trial, saying the lawyer was…

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday defended her lead defense counsel, Sheila Sison, against accusations of bullying from a private prosecutor in her impeachment trial, saying the lawyer was being unfairly vilified for doing her job.

Duterte's statement came a day after private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan called Sison a bully and accused her of disrespecting the prosecution and the senator-judges after the defense described the impeachment proceedings as “persecution.”

“Lorna Kapunan calling a defense counsel a bully is like calling David the aggressor against Goliath. It is a convenient way to vilify the person defending against an overwhelming display of political power,” Duterte said.
Duterte cited the defense team's long hours and personal sacrifices in preparing for the impeachment trial.

“What exactly is the defense counsel’s role in these alleged political transactions? None. She is simply doing her job. Since 2023, the defense team has devoted countless hours to preparing for this case, sacrificing sleep, family time, and peace of mind to study documents and prepare their defense,” Duterte added.
The House inquiry into Duterte's use of confidential funds, however, began only in September 2024.
Duterte reiterated that she was being politically persecuted through the impeachment proceedings.

“If impeachment and the national budget are being used as instruments of political survival of the corrupt, then it is the people, not the defense counsel, who are being taken for granted,” Duterte said.

Duterte was responding to remarks Kapunan made at a post-hearing press conference on Tuesday, when the private prosecutor accused Sison of bullying the prosecution by repeatedly using terms such as “persecution,” “accused” and “denial of due process” in her statements before the impeachment court.

Kapunan also expressed dismay over the ruling of Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, who denied the prosecution's motion to strike Sison's use of the word “persecution” from the record.

“The ruling of the presiding officer to let it (persecution remark remain), I think it's not fair. In my years of practice, I know what bullying is. I am a defender of those who are victims of bullying. And that's exactly what the head defense counsel always does to us,” Kapunan said.
Kapunan accused Sison of using her statements before the impeachment court to question the fairness of the proceedings and portray Duterte as a victim of persecution.

“She bullies us and inserts into her manifestations words like persecution, words like accused [instead of respondent Vice President], words like denial of due process, words like there is no fairness and justice here,” she added.

“She (Sison) is a bully. And there is no place for bullying in a Senate impeachment court. Not only that, hindi lang bullying, gagamitin ko na yung word, bastos. Binabastos niya, hindi lang ang prosecution, pati ang senator judges as she did today. Huwag naman,” Kapunan said.
(She is disrespectful, not only to the prosecution but also to the senator-judges. She should stop that.)

The dispute arose during Tuesday's impeachment court proceedings, when Sison described the case against Duterte as “persecution” while objecting to the prosecution's decision to drop three of the four Articles of Impeachment against the Vice President.

“I would take that the November 9 resumption of hearing [for the defense presentation of evidence] is not really to presume that the prosecution or persecution of the respondent will continue on set dates,” Sison said.

The prosecution had presented evidence on Article 1, which concerns the alleged misuse of confidential funds, and Article 4, which involves alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

The prosecution's decision to drop three articles left Article 2 as the remaining charge to be pursued. It alleges that Duterte had unexplained wealth because of the non-declaration of assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) and her failure to divest business interests despite a constitutional prohibition.

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro moved to strike Sison's use of the word “persecution” from the record, saying both sides should observe proper decorum and courtesy despite being adverse parties.

“We hope that the impeachment court will remind the defense that while we are adverse parties we are bound to extend the necessary decorum and courtesy in this impeachment court. I move to strike persecution [word] which was used three times by the defense from the transcript of records of the honorable impeachment court,” Luistro said.
Luistro also said the prosecution's painstaking efforts to present credible evidence should not be dismissed as mere “persecution.”

“On the use of persecution, we take offense to that. It is totally unfair on the part of the volunteer lawyers who are leaving their private practice just to be here to support the public prosecutors. It is totally unfair for all the people helping the prosecution team, exhibiting their dedication and hard work in preparing and presenting evidence before the impeachment court,” Luistro added.
Escudero denied the motion, allowing the remark to remain on record.

“Let it remain as it is. It is a description from the point of view of the respondent [as indicated in her written answer], and how they (defense) view the complaint filed against their client,” Escudero said.— MCG, GMA News
