articles.title: ICC rejects Duterte camp bid to cap evidence at 10,000 items
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has rejected former president Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team’s request to limit the prosecution’s evidence to 10,000 items in his crimes against…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 14, 2026 | 11:03am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on Oct. 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) has rejected former president Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team’s request to limit the prosecution’s evidence to 10,000 items in his crimes against humanity of murder case over killings linked to his administration’s anti-drug campaign.

Duterte attended the fourth status conference on Tuesday, October 13, as the ICC Trial Chamber III denied the defense’s request for the prosecution to refile its evidence in a new case file in the Judicial Workflow Platform (JWP), the court’s digital system for managing case records and evidence.
“Your motion that the evidence should be refiled in JWP and the prosecution limited to 10,000 documents is at the moment refused,” Korner said.

Korner said the proposed new case file and evidence cap could violate the prosecution’s disclosure obligations. She advised prosecutors to identify exculpatory evidence and urged Duterte’s lead counsel, Peter Haynes, to provide search terms to help locate materials relevant to the defense.
Haynes said he and prosecutor Julian Nicholls had maintained regular communication and cooperation in handling the case.
Nicholls, however, said prosecutors had asked the defense for search terms but had yet to receive them.

He proposed appointing an independent expert to review the evidence and suggested that both sides agree on documents confirming deaths during police operations to establish the number of killings reflected in the dataset without examining every document.
Evidence dispute

In a motion filed in September, Duterte’s defense team asked the ICC to cap the prosecution’s evidence at 10,000 items, arguing that the volume of materials disclosed ahead of trial would hamper its preparation.

The defense said the prosecution’s evidence had grown from 5,275 items during the confirmation phase to 62,130 items. It also cited more than 320,000 pages of documents and 1,000 audio-visual materials.

The status conference came after the ICC ruled that Duterte was fit to stand trial. The tribunal’s decision, made public on October 8, cleared the way for the proceedings to begin as scheduled on November 30.

Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity involving alleged murders and attempted murders committed in the Philippines between November 2011 and March 2019, according to the charges filed by prosecutors.
The case stems from the ICC’s investigation into alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during Duterte’s anti-drug campaign.
Duterte was arrested in Manila in March 2025 and surrendered to the ICC on March 12, 2025. He remains detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen, The Hague, Netherlands.

articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Commuters and motorists brave heavy rains along United Nations Avenue in Manila.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Visayas and Mindanao may experience rains due to the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), the state weather bureau PAGASA said.
In its weather forecast on Wednesday, October 14, PAGASA said that Visayas and Mindanao may expect cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the ITCZ.
The state weather bureau warned residents of these areas of possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to, at times, heavy rains.
Meanwhile, Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region and Cagayan Valley may expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated light rains due to northeasterly windflow.
Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon may also expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
PAGASA also reported that it is monitoring a tropical depression outside of the Philippine area of responsibility.
The weather system is estimated to be at 2,340 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon, as of 3 a.m. on Monday.

articles.title: Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
articles.summary: Ten years after the series finale, the "Girls" are getting back together to explore the "milestone of turning forty", HBO says.

blocks.text: HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.

Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars – shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells.

All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer.
"We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement.
"I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said.
"Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said.
Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting.
It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s.
The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century.
"We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said.

"To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."
The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".
Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.
In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.

In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival.
Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude.
"I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.
Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.

articles.title: ’How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’ Why Indian voters are on the streets
articles.summary:
Anger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Shaikh Azizur Rahman

blocks.text: Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.

The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.

blocks.caption: Shahida Fakir is staying in a village in Bangladesh after she was detained on suspicion of being an illegal immigrant and pushed across the border. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.

Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.

In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.

On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.

Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.

The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.

Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.

In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”

blocks.caption: A protest march in Dhaka, Bangladesh, against India’s ‘push-ins’ of Muslims at the border in June. Photograph: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.

“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.

Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.

“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”

blocks.caption: BJP supporters celebrate during vote counting at state elections in West Bengal in May 2026. Photograph: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
after newsletter promotion

“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.

By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.

Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.

“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”

Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.

Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”

None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”

The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.

Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.

A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”
Additional reporting Aakash Hassan

"The withdrawal is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning," Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for Duterte, said in a statement.

"Yet, it is also an injustice and a denial of due process because it deprives the Vice President of the opportunity to confront these charges and present countervailing evidence in the proper forum, which is the Senate Impeachment Court," he said.
"More than that, it deprived her of the vindication of the acquittal she deserves if the Court ruled only on the basis of evidence and law," Panelo added.
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero made the ruling after the prosecution told the Senate court that it will no longer pursue the three Articles of Impeachment and will only retain one: Article 2 on amassing of unexplained wealth due to failure to disclose assets in the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) and non-divestment of business interests despite Constitutional prohibition. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Grad student accused of trying to flee U.S. after police questioned her about alleged poisoning
articles.summary: A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents, then tried to flee the U.S. after police questioned…

image.caption: A March 2012 file photo shows the University of Wyoming campus sign in Laramie, Wyo. (Andy Carpenean/Laramie Boomerang/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents, then tried to flee the U.S. after police questioned her.
Microbiology grad student alleged to have poisoned tea of University of Wyoming colleague

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were "multiple" laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police.

Investigators say Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the alleged victim, who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work Wang had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles.

items: Woman at centre of Cornell gang-rape case was 'misled' about investigation, lawyer says

blocks.text: It's claimed the poison was first detected when the wife of the alleged victim and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations have left him reeling. He said he was uncertain if the alleged victim will fully recover.

"It's been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student's life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that," Gomelsky told The Associated Press. "That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career."
Wang has no attorney listed in court documents. The Associated Press tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
Surveillance in shared office space

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as K.T., began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical acrylamide in the coffee maker's water.
K.T. and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie, Wyo.

Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through K.T.'s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded "taking photos and manipulating notebooks" on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer's affidavit said.

items: Disgraced former Manitoba law dean racked up millions in Swiss debt ahead of France arrest, documents suggest

blocks.text: Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
Police said Wang had asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer.
A carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide, which can be acutely toxic in high doses, is also used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she "had not used acrylamide in years."

A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of "multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials," according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to "significantly increase" her $200,000 US bond upon extradition.

Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved "new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment," according to the affidavit.
Wang "was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.," the affidavit alleges.
Envied colleague's success, prof says
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.

Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague's success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a conference in August, Gomelsky said.
Later that month he went to the campus health clinic with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness.
The student also said he had noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said, and that when he washed the coffee maker the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

The water from the coffee maker was boiled down to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit. The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.
Unclear if alleged victim will recover

Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is "not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere," Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on "a pretty promising cancer therapy method," Sumaya added.

items: 'An unfortunate accident': Calgary woman accused of killing security guard walks away from manslaughter charge

blocks.text: The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
"Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it's unclear if he'll fully recover or not," the professor said.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 US fine.
It's not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors' request and raised bond to $1.5 million US, cash only.

articles.title: Russia detains Japanese journalist, accusing him of alleged spying
articles.summary:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east…

blocks.text: Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.

Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.

Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.

The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.

Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.

“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.

Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan. Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
articles.summary: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia.

blocks.text: The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.
The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.
Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".
Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.
"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."
He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.

One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.
Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".

"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."
He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," she said.
Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.
His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.
He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.
"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.
"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."

Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.
The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.
Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.
In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.
With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

articles.title: Canadian health reporter Helen Branswell dead at 69, remembered as 'pretty kickass' journalist
articles.summary: Helen Branswell, a journalist celebrated for her years of coverage on public health and infectious diseases, has died at the age of 69.

image.caption: Veteran Canadian health and medicine reporter Helen Branswell, seen on stage at the 2024 STAT Summit in Boston, died in an Ottawa hospital on Tuesday, following a highly-respected career in journalism that spanned more than four decades. (Sarah Gonzalez/STAT)

blocks.text: Health·New
Helen Branswell, a journalist celebrated for her years of coverage on public health and infectious diseases, has died at the age of 69.
Renowned Quebec-born Branwell known for coverage of public health threats from COVID-19 to Ebola
Helen Branswell, a journalist celebrated for her decades of coverage of public health and infectious diseases, has died at the age of 69.
The Sherbrooke, Que.-born reporter died Tuesday, according to an article from STAT, the Boston-based health and medicine news site she had worked for since its founding in 2015.
Her sister, Brenda Branswell, confirmed to the outlet she died of complications from cancer. She had moved back to Canada last year, after a decade in Boston, to be closer to family, STAT reported.
"She loved her work," Brenda Branswell told STAT. "She loved science and medical writing. She thought her job was a gift. She found it so interesting."
Branswell's fellow journalists, members of the medical community and some of the world's top health officials are mourning the loss of a revered reporter.
Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said he was among those "privileged to work with Helen over many years."

"Throughout her career, Helen demonstrated an unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth, helping the public understand some of the most complex and consequential health challenges of our time," he wrote in a post on the social media platform X.
"At a moment when misinformation competes with facts, her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty and insight," he wrote.
Former CBC News journalist Kelly Crowe recalled how Branswell was "always conscious of her duty to inform the public without alarming them."
An acclaimed journalist by chance

Branswell was widely recognized for her reporting at STAT and, previously, during 29 years with The Canadian Press — as a reporter in Ottawa, Calgary and Halifax, a European correspondent and, finally, medical reporter, according to her LinkedIn profile.
It was at the latter news company where "she got hooked on infectious disease reporting covering the 2003 SARS-1 outbreak in Toronto," according to her biography on STAT's website.

Branswell and her STAT colleagues were finalists for the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for their coverage of COVID-19. She separately won the 2020 George Polk Journalism Award for Public Service for documenting the first year of the pandemic.
She wrote 161 stories that year, beginning on Jan. 4, 2020, when she reported on a mystery pneumonia outbreak in China that could be the result of "a new virus, and perhaps even a new coronavirus."
Her final piece, a contribution to STAT's Morning Rounds newsletter about the growing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, was published on Oct. 2.
As recently as Monday, Branswell was updating her colleagues in a Slack channel from her hospital bed with data about maternal RSV vaccine uptake, STAT reported.
Although colleagues are reflecting on her long and dedicated career, Branswell said it was "by complete serendipity" that she found her way into journalism.

She explained in 2022, when Carleton University awarded Branswell an honorary doctorate in recognition of her career and "stellar coverage" of the pandemic, that she didn't really know what she wanted to do with her life after she graduated from St. Thomas University in Fredericton, N.B., with a bachelor of arts in English literature.
But she ultimately landed a reporting gig with The Daily Gleaner newspaper in Fredericton, opening the door to a career she described as "highly fulfilling and rewarding."
Trusted journalist, wonderful person and 'pretty kickass'
STAT described Branswell's role as infectious diseases correspondent as "inherently unpredictable," but one that earned her a loyal following of readers and the respect of leading health officials.
Maria Van Kerkhove, the WHO's director of epidemic and pandemic management, thanked Branswell on social media for her "extraordinary reporting, rigor and humanity."
Van Kerkhove told STAT she "always wanted to have a conversation with Helen," praising her thoughtful questions on complex topics and describing her as "pretty kickass, and no nonsense."

Branswell could be counted on for her "brilliant, ethical, evidence-based" journalism, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, said Dr. Peter Jay Hotez, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston.
"She never fell for the ridiculous conspiracies or raised false equivalencies just to get more clicks and readers," Hotez said on X. "Helen was very special, I will miss her."

STAT owner and co-founder John W. Henry said Branswell was someone everyone at the outlet could lean on for any number of issues and that her death was a loss "for everyone who cares about health and medicine."
"Beyond that she was a wonderful person," he wrote in a note to staff, according to STAT.
Crowe applauded Branswell's diligence and how she continued reporting on vital stories long after they faded from the headlines.

"It's as though she never slept. She was always on top of alll of the files in her beat," Crowe wrote in an email to CBC News. "And when a new development occurred she had it — usually first — and with precision, accuracy and context."
CBC Radio's Dr. Brian Goldman, host of White Coat, Black Art and The Dose, called Branswell "one of the best medical journalists of her generation."
"Canada's own made it big in the U.S. during COVID. May her memory be a blessing."

Nick Logan is a senior writer with CBC based in Vancouver. He is a multi-platform reporter and producer, with a particular focus on international news. You can reach out to him at nick.logan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
articles.summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.

blocks.text: Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.
Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.
He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.

In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.

Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.

Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.

"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.

In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.

In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.

Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

blocks.text: NBA·New

Kawhi Leonard received the loudest ovation during team introductions as he made his re-debut for the Toronto Raptors. Leonard was in the starting lineup as Toronto hosted the New York Knicks in a pre-season game on Tuesday night.
Star forward features in starting lineup against defending champion Knicks in Toronto
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 13, 2026 7:35 PM EDT | Last Updated: 25 minutes ago
Kawhi Leonard received the loudest ovation during team introductions as he made his re-debut for the Toronto Raptors.

Leonard was in the starting lineup as Toronto hosted the New York Knicks in a pre-season game on Tuesday night. It's the two-time NBA Finals MVP's first game for the Raptors since he was traded by the Los Angeles Clippers back to Toronto this past off-season.

"His minutes are going to be limited, but it's going to be super important to get him there with our guys on the court, to get him integrated," said Raptors head coach Darko Rajakovic in a pre-game media availability. "It's very special that it's happening right here at home, not on some road game, but actually playing in front of our fans in Toronto.
"I think it's a very special day for him. Very special day for us. We're super excited to get him on the floor and to play."
KAWHIIIII 👌 https://t.co/GU6Ki3Z39S—Raptors

Leonard had previously played for the Raptors in the 2018-19 season, leading them to their only NBA championship. He then signed a lucrative free-agent deal to join his hometown Clippers the following off-season.

L.A. traded him back to Toronto this past summer in a deal delayed by an NBA investigation into Leonard and the Clippers for salary cap circumvention. Although the team, its owner Steve Ballmer and several executives were severely punished by the league, Leonard only received a relatively small fine.

Once the punishments were doled out the trade was able to go through, sending Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, a 2027 pick swap and two second-round selections to Los Angeles.

items: Kawhi Leonard is a Raptor again. Are we sure that's a good thing?
Happy in return to Raptors, Kawhi Leonard doesn't regret leaving after winning 2019 NBA title

blocks.text: Leonard averaged 27.9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 3.6 assists, 1.9 steals and 0.4 blocks over 65 regular-season games last season for the Clippers.
The goal? Have fun

"Goal for him tonight is to go out there and have a lot of fun. That's the number 1 thing," said Rajakovic, noting that Leonard had been with L.A. for seven seasons. "I don't expect that he's going to pick up on terminology or all the stuff.
"We're teaching him a lot, showing a lot of film, going through a lot of drills and whatnot. Once the ball goes in the air, he just needs to play basketball."

The defending NBA champion Knicks had lost all three of their pre-season games heading into Tuesday's game at Scotiabank Arena. Toronto was 1-1, with three pre-season games left on the Raptors schedule including the game against New York.
Toronto will host the Chicago Bulls on Oct. 21 in their home opener.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
articles.summary: Simbarashe Kundizeza was responding to an accusation that has caused an uproar on social media.

blocks.text: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external.
The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.

"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme.

The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday.

It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.
The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external.
Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external.
Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.
"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external.
"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.

Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external.
In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.
Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.
She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".
Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".
"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."

Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".

In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers.
The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".

Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."

In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."
For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.
"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.
"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.

The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.
"Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday.
On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write."

articles.title: Sandiganbayan acquits Garin in Dengvaxia vaccine case
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Special Second Division has acquitted former Health Secretary and now House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin and several other health officials of graft and technical malversation…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 14, 2026 | 7:30am
In this photo uploaded on Facebook on May 6, 2026 shows Rep. Janette Garin (Iloilo 1st District) at the main session hall of the House of Representatives.
Janette Garin via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Special Second Division has acquitted former health secretary and now House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin and several other health officials of graft and technical malversation charges in connection with the controversial P3.55-billion procurement of Dengvaxia vaccines in 2015.

In a 43-page decision promulgated on October 13, the anti-graft court cleared Garin and her co-accused of all criminal charges, citing the prosecution's failure to prove their guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The cases stemmed from the health department's realignment of government funds and the subsequent issuance of a Special Allotment Release Order on Dec. 29, 2015, which allocated P3,556,155,900.00 for the procurement of Dengvaxia vaccines under the government's School-Based Immunization Program.

The prosecution argued that the accused acted in "evident bad faith" and in open defiance of Executive Order No. 49, series of 1993, which mandates that government drug procurements must be listed in the Philippine National Drug Formulary.
However, the Sandiganbayan ruled that the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence of a "fraudulent and dishonest purpose."
The court noted that the Department of Health had a valid mechanism for securing exemptions from the Philippine National Drug Formulary for national health programs.
Furthermore, the anti-graft court highlighted testimonies from the Commission on Audit confirming that no public funds were missing from the transaction.

“Whatever the adverse consequences of the Dengvaxia vaccines administered to schoolchildren may be, the Court cannot find sufficient link that such unfortunate incidents were motivated by evil or sinister design by the program implementors, mainly by the accused,” the anti-graft court said.

On the charge of technical malversation, the court ruled that the third element of the crime — that public funds were applied to a use different from what they were originally appropriated for by law — was not present.

The Sandiganbayan pointed out that while Garin requested the use of savings to fund the urgent dengue vaccination program, the legal authority to declare and transfer savings within the executive branch rests solely with the President of the Philippines under the Constitution and the 2015 GAA.
The court noted that then-President Benigno Aquino III, through then-Budget Secretary Florencio Abad, approved the fund augmentation from the 2015 Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund (MPBF).

"In the final analysis, the one who caused the application of the savings from the 2015 MPBF to the purchase of dengue vaccines was none other than the President, and not accused Garin. The buck stops with the President, so to speak, and not with the member of his cabinet," the court ruled.

Additionally, the court clarified that Garin’s co-accused could not be held liable for technical malversation as they were not "accountable public officers" who had custody or possession of the funds under the law.

articles.title: Cornell suspends frat parties after gang rape case
articles.summary: Cornell said no parties will be held at frat houses until the end of the academic year. The university is trying to mend its reputation following its handling of a gang rape case in 2024.

image.caption: Cornell University will take several measures in response to the 2024 gang rape caseImage: Ted Shaffrey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cornell University has suspended all parties at frat houses until the end of the 2026/27 academic year, the university announced on Tuesday.

This comes after the case in which a woman alleged to have been drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, with the university's reaction to the gang rape allegations now attracting criticizm from around the nation and overseas.
The new measures include a new "zero tolerance" policy for violations, which would result in an immediate suspension of a chapter.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said these measures were to "provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life" at Cornell, while also determining how it can safely continue. The university has more than 20 active fraternities that are organized under its Interfraternity Council.
It is not clear whether the suspension also includes parties that take place outside the campus.
More support for victims

As part of the measures, Cornell is to hold talks with students and faculty experts about the "the development of safe social alternatives" to Greek life party culture, as well as investing the money needed to support the initiatives' establishment, Kotlikoff said.
The Cornell president also said the institution will be adding a case manager to its Office of Civil Rights to support people that report sexual misconduct to help in navigating the process.

Campus police, which has full law enforcement authority but is controlled by Cornell, are largely the ones responsible for looking into crimes committed at the university. However, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell will work closely with New York State Police to allow an investigation independent of the school.

blocks.caption: The case triggered widespread protests across the USImage: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Decision not to prosecute criticized

The 2024 gang rape allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was lader met with widespread criticizm.
The woman filed a lawsuit in September, in which she claimed she had been drugged and sexually assaulted by several fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.
According to the lawsuit, messages saying she was sexually available were sent among fraternity members without her knowledge.

blocks.caption: The Chi Phi fraternity house, where the woman was allegedly assaultedImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.
All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied the allegations.

After the case was made public and triggered wide-scale criticism, the investigation is now in the hands of New York Attorney General Letitia James. The university's response will be reviewed by former Deputy US Attorney General Sally Yates.
