articles.title: Man who died in Six Flags rollercoaster fall in Georgia was a father and educator
articles.summary:
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was a father of 10-year-old daughter, and overcame two bouts of cancer, his family says

Police on Tuesday identified the victim of the

blocks.text: Police on Tuesday identified the victim of the fatal accident at Six Flags Over Georgia as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta.
Kariem fell to his death after being ejected from his seat and several others were injured in an incident involving a rollercoaster at the theme park.
Although authorities and Six Flags did not identify the rollercoaster, video footage shows passengers being evacuated from the park’s Goliath coaster.
Kariem was a father to a 10-year-old daughter and an educator in Atlanta, Georgia.
According to Atlanta public schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an IT Manager.
“Atlanta Public Schools extends its deepest condolences to the family, friends, and loved ones of Mr Kariem,” a spokesperson for APS shared in a statement obtained by the Guardian.

“He was a cherished member of the Wesley International Academy and APS families whose presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched,” the statement added.
Wesley International Academy did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment.
Kariem’s family spoke with 11Alive’s Chase Houle, and shared that he overcame many challenges in life, including two bouts of cancer. The last stint was in 2018.
Additionally, his family said Kariem and his daughter survived a car fire three weeks ago. The two were unharmed in the incident.
Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation into Kariem’s death.
It was unknown what led to the fatal accident, nor how the others were injured or their conditions.
Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US.

The incident comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in southern California announced the permanent closure of its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injuries caused by the ride.
The park had settled one wrongful death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed rollercoaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental.
According to a local Atlanta news station, Six Flags Over Georgia remains closed because of the offseason schedule and was expected to reopen on Friday.

articles.title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
articles.summary: Some fear the government's standoff with the former PM's supporters could bring more instability, not less.

blocks.text: Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town.

Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less.
According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror.

"The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon.
Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored.
While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding.
On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area.
To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental.
For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release.
"The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House.

"I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party."
The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody.
Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September, accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since.

Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years.

The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated.
With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities?

"The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government."
The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics.

Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion.
But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party.
"The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says.
Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision.
"The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says.

Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks.
"The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally."
But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most.

The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India.
Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous.

Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame.

"I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands."
"It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan.
Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues.

"If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds.
Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour.
"It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says.

"Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open.
"Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it."

articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.

blocks.text: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.

Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".

There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.

blocks.text: Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.

Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.

"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

blocks.text: Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.

There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.

blocks.text: Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.

"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.

Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.

"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.

blocks.text: Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.

"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.

blocks.text: Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.

"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.

"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
articles.summary: Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Wildfires have been raging in Kalimantan, Indonesia for weeks
ByKoh Ewe
Reporting fromSingapore
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.

The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.

But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".

Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.
Watch: What makes fires in Indonesia so hard to extinguish?
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.

This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.

First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.

The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.

But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.

Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".

Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
Watch: Toxic smog makes thousands sick as Indonesia wildfires rage
But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.

In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.

"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.
"The government must also think about the common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."

articles.title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

blocks.text: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.

He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

articles.title: Florida officials say six people dead from Hurricane Isaias
articles.summary:
Governor Ron DeSantis says death toll ‘sad’ but praises work of local officials for helping to minimize storm’s impact

Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane…

blocks.text: Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias.

In a press conference on Tuesday, Florida governor Ron DeSantis praised the work of local officials for minimizing the impact of the storm, which made landfall late on Friday, ⁠bringing strong winds, rain, flash floods and tornado ​threats across parts of the ​US south-east, leaving hundreds of thousands ​of residents without power.
DeSantis confirmed that there are six deaths linked to Hurricane Isaias, including two previously confirmed deaths.
One person was killed after a fallen tree on a home resulted in a direct fatality. Another individual was found deceased in their garage with a running generator in Escambia county.
DeSantis confirmed that the remaining deaths linked to the storm include a car accident at an intersection, and storm-related disruptions to two people’s medical treatment.

Despite there being half a dozen of deaths, the governor praised Floridians and local officials for taking proper precautions, linking it to there being a lower death toll, compared to previous storms.

“We’re sad to hear that. At the same time, we’ve had some where there have been a lot more. So I think that people did take precautions and I think the local officials did a good job of spreading the word,” DeSantis said Tuesday.
There are about 5,000 people in Florida state that remain without power north-west of where the storm landed, according to DeSantis.
Free supplies are being provided at different locations of distribution to Floridians that have been impacted by the hurricane.

Isaias is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season. As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is also the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) said there is increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surges along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi.

articles.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
articles.summary: A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.

image.caption: A listening device was found late last month, OpenAI saidImage: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices.

A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing.
The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Will AI destroy humanity?
How was the device found?
OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect.

"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added.
According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room."

He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device.

Tech firm says FBI now investigating and an arrest has been made

OpenAI CEO tells world leaders to help guide AI's future

blocks.text: World
Nationwide protests by high school students over education in France in recent weeks have spread to other parts of Europe.
Weeks of protest over school conditions, education costs spread to Albania, Greece
Nationwide protests by high school students over education in France have spread to other parts of Europe in recent weeks.
In Albania
Student organizers in Albania said Tuesday's nationwide protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at Albania's Education Ministry in Tirana, and police fired tear gas and water cannons in response as the demonstration turned violent.
(Florion Goga/Reuters)
Police officers detained several protesters.
In France

High school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades in France, demanding more teachers and better facilities. Below, they, along with teachers and parents, block a street near the Lycée Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Tuesday.
(Abdul Saboor/Reuters)
More than 161,000 people took to the streets of major French cities, according to Interior Ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.

While most demonstrators marched peacefully, riot police charged protesters and fired tear gas in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalized property and hurled objects at police.

articles.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant 'danger to community,' prosecution argues
articles.summary: Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, has argued that Bryant poses a flight risk and a danger to the public, and should not be granted bail. He…

image.caption: A district court judge in Seattle is set to hear arguments about whether alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant should be granted bail. (Lois Silver/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, has argued that Bryant poses a flight risk and a danger to the public, and should not be granted bail. He says there are substance abuse issues and mental health concerns that should also be factored in.
Seattle court will hear arguments regarding bail Tuesday afternoon
A district court judge in Seattle will determine whether alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant should be granted bail Tuesday.

Bryant, a 30-year-old resident of Bellingham, Wash. — whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody — was arrested Oct. 6 and charged with one count of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Prosecutors say that conspiracy involved encouraging and supporting Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar in the lead-up to the Feb. 10 attack, in which she killed five students and one staff member at the campus, after shooting and killing her mother and stepbrother at their home.
Police allege that in online interactions on the social media platform Discord, Bryant agreed to livestream the attack, gave Van Rootselaar money, and provided months of logistical support.
Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, has argued that Bryant poses a flight risk and a danger to the public, and should not be granted bail.
The home of alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator James Cody Bryant in Bellingham, Wash. (Caroline Barghout/CBC)
"It does not get much more serious or dangerous for the community," he said in a memorandum filed Tuesday in support of a detention order.

"Bryant’s participation in the charged murder conspiracy took place primarily through online communications … There are simply no conditions of release that can be fully and effectively enforced to ensure that Bryant does not pose a continuing threat to the community through online behavior."
Efforts to assist in shooting
Tuesday's memorandum drew on conversations alleged to have taken place between Bryant and Van Rootselaar as the attack was planned.

On Feb. 9, the day before the shooting, Van Rootselaar reportedly told Bryant she didn't want to carry out the shooting if she didn't "know for certain" someone would livestream it, the court documents outline.

items: Disturbing new details of Tumbler Ridge shooting plans revealed in court documents

blocks.text: "I literally fixed my sleep schedule to help me stay up to be there after work," Bryant replied.
According to the memorandum, a livestream was initiated in the moments before the attack but failed after about 20 seconds due to technical issues.
"The livestream’s failure was despite Bryant’s best efforts to make it happen," Greenberg said.

Greenberg also pointed to a payment of $14.33 Bryant sent to Van Rootselaar's PayPal ID to enable her to purchase a lighter to ignite an explosive device constructed for use in the attack. The payment was reversed because the account had been deactivated.
The District of Tumbler Ridge town hall as pictured on Aug. 21, 2026. (Tom Summer/CBC)
"Van Rootselaar ultimately deployed this explosive device," Greenberg said.

"Although $14.33 may not be a lot of money, it speaks volumes about the seriousness of the offense and the defendant’s character that Bryant was willing to help purchase the ignition source for an explosive device that was to be used to attack schoolchildren."

He also argued substance abuse and mental health concerns should be factored in, including evidence of suicidal ideations that were shared with Van Rootselaar but not disclosed to the Probation Office.

items: U.S. resident's actions 'helped facilitate' Tumbler Ridge attack: RCMP asst. commissioner | Hanomansing Live

blocks.text: "Bryant repeatedly acknowledged being in a unique position to stop Van Rootselaar," he said.

"Anyone whose character allows them to help plan a mass shooting and then sits back and (literally) tries to watch as schoolchildren are murdered … is a danger to the community and should be detained pending trial."
Defense argues for conditional release

In their application opposing a motion for detention, assistant federal public defenders Gregory Murphy and Dennis Carroll argued Bryant had co-operated with investigators in the days following the attack.
"She expressed horror at Van Rootselaar’s crimes," they said.
The defence argued that law enforcement had acknowledged Bryant repeatedly tried to dissuade Van Rootselaar from carrying out the attack, and pointed to their client's clean criminal record.
"There is no evidence that she has ever personally committed an act of violence. There is no evidence that she is in contact with anyone else planning an act of violence," Murphy and Carroll said.
Defense counsel underscored Bryant's stable residence, close ties to the community, and long-term employment at a local McDonald's restaurant.
In his submission, Greenberg said Bryant had admitted to being "on thin ice" at work due to repeatedly calling in sick.

items: Alleged use of Discord to plan Tumbler Ridge shooting comes under scrutiny

blocks.text: "It’s not clear whether that job remains available due to the arrest in this case," he said.

Murphy and Carroll also disputed Greenberg's mental health concerns, arguing that although Bryant had "briefly" seen a psychologist during high school and had taken medication for panic attacks, there was no evidence to support claims of suicidality.
"There is no evidence she has expressed a thought of harming herself in the last fourteen months. There is no evidence she ever has made plans to hurt herself," the application read.
They said Bryant did not have connections to any other countries and had no means by which to flee.
"The Court should release Ms. Bryant on conditions, which may include home detention, a mental health assessment, and strict limitations on her use of the internet," the defense team said.
More to come.

The Josh Frydenberg book-promotion/comeback-to-politics tour continues.
The former treasurer, and ousted member for Kooyong, appeared on 7:30 last night, again raising the possibility of his return to frontline politics.
His memoir, A Grateful Son, is the Trojan Horse that legitimises questions like: “Do you think you’d make a good prime minister?”

“Look, I haven’t closed the door to reentering politics,” Frydenberg reiterated. “That would involve running for a seat, winning it, joining the party room and then proceeding after that. So there are a lot of steps.”

Frydenberg: “Look, I think it’s important to know what you believe in, and I certainly do, to have policy ideas that can take the country in the right direction, and to be consistent with the philosophy and the values of our great party, and that’s what I articulate in the book.”
